intent: Create the confirmed Caldris world, The Measure of Mercy campaign, and its reviewed opening places so the world is selectable in the D&D 2024 website.

value.summary: A low-magic medieval world of wet roads, toll bridges, walled market towns, river kingdoms, warm ports, old grudges, rare wonders, and two continents facing one another across the Lantern Sea.

value.title: The Measure of Mercy
value.premise: A bridge toll and a bell that rings thirteen times lead from local corruption to royal succession, transcontinental archives, and the old responsibility of a dragon—without losing sight of supper, friendship, weather, work, and ordinary lives worth protecting.
partyGoals: Become part of Bramblebridge without taking over its life.
Learn who profits from the new toll orders and why an empty tax wagon reached the market.
Choose how powerful systems can be made humane without making every victory belong to one conspiracy.
toneAndBoundaries: Cozy, lightly humorous, storybook medieval adventure grounded in believable work, law, travel, weather, and consequence.
Magic is rare and remarkable rather than ordinary infrastructure; grief and danger appear beside warmth, eccentricity, and recovery.
Mysteries reward secrets, riddles, conversation, and creative solutions; apparent bosses may reveal higher layers while completed adventures still matter.

value.summary: The western continent: a green-and-grey patchwork of river kingdoms, cold moors, sea cliffs, orchards, monasteries, old imperial roads, and mountains hiding exhausted mines and older obligations.

The eastern and southeastern continent: deltas, dry plateaus, terraced highlands, island chains, caravan rivers, shaded courts, white-stone ports, and societies shaped by canals, cisterns, sailing seasons, and river law.

Alderwick's rain-polished market town where the old Lantern Road crosses the narrow Weir, serving twelve villages, three mills, Mallow Abbey, and a weekly market famous for onions, wool, second-hand books, and arguments about awnings.
A settlement of raised paths and low marsh islands where ferries, reed craft, smoked eel, practical flood knowledge, dry socks, and gossip are all taken seriously.
A quarry village beneath singing cliffs, supplying pale building stone and slate while warm air rises from a reopened face that intersects something built rather than natural.
Bramblebridge's warm timber inn: copper pots, crowded common tables, excellent dumplings, wet cloaks, a permanently crooked stair, and letters addressed to an inn that burned ninety years ago.
The civic bell, market clock, pigeon roost, and best view in town; its rope was cut before the noon bell rang thirteen times by itself, according to three mutually incompatible witnesses.
